thread.title_full: Indiana Senate prepares to vote on redistricting bill - NewsBreak

author: Hannah Adamson
title: Indiana Senate prepares to vote on redistricting bill - NewsBreak
text:
By Hannah Adamson ,
1 hours ago
INDIANAPOLIS — After a contentious back-and-forth over the past five months, the Indiana Senate is less than 24 hours away from deciding whether to pass a new congressional map.
“I’m going to do what’s right, and let the chips fall where they may,” State Sen. Dan Dernulc (R-Highland) said.
“This is democracy in action, and I think we’ve given a lot of people opportunity to weigh in,” State Sen. Andy Zay (R-Huntington) said.
Sen. Zay, who supports redistricting efforts, and Sen. Dernulc, who has not said how he’ll vote on Thursday, are two of 12 Senate Republicans who have been targeted in a series of bomb threats, swatting incidents, and other acts of intimidation over the past few weeks.
“Our phones have been very busy and, you know, kudos to so many citizens for Indiana for weighing in on the issue and, you know, we’ll see how the day goes and see if we can wrap it up tomorrow,” Sen. Zay said.
Wednesday, the Senate passed HB 1032 on its second reading. Senate Democrats introduced three amendments—all of which failed. One amendment would have stripped the bill entirely and replaced it with a ban on mid-cycle redistricting.
“I’m extremely disappointed that we spent five months talking about one piece of legislation that impacts one person in Washington, D.C., at the expense of 6.8 million people in Indiana who are asking for affordability every single day,” State Sen. Fady Qaddoura (D-Indianapolis) said.
Late Wednesday night, the Greater Indianapolis NAACP called on senators to vote no on HB 1032. A statement from NAACP President/CEO Derrick Johnson reads in part:
“Redistricting should serve the people—not political insiders. Mid-decade map changes erode public trust and disproportionately harm communities that are already fighting to be heard. Indiana must remain committed to a fair and transparent process that protects every voter’s voice.”
Senate Majority Whip Michael Crider (R-Greenfield) told reporters following Wednesday’s Senate session that the majority of his district opposes redistricting and that he would vote no on Thursday.
“Look at Georgia, which created maps which that were supposed to advantage Republicans, and they just lost a safe Republican seat,” Sen. Crider said. “I think that you can make some changes, like we’re talking about and end up with a result that you didn’t expect at all.”
Sen. Crider also said he’s received three threats of violence this week alone.
“A lot of tactics that have been used, the threats, my home is supposed to be firebombed and shoot everybody in the house as we flee the house…to me, this has been a really kind of discouraging thing that we’re experiencing this in Indiana,” Sen. Crider said.
According to Sen. Crider, the votes still aren’t there to move the proposal forward.
“I still hold that position that I don’t think the votes are there to pass it,” Sen. Crider said.
Indiana Senate President Pro Tem Rod Bray (R-Martinsville) had previously said the votes weren’t there, but told reporters on Monday that the final vote has yet to be determined.
“What I’m saying right now is we’re all going to find out together on Thursday,” Sen. Bray said.
In a post to Truth Social Wednesday night, President Trump criticized Sen. Bray, saying in part:
“…Rod Bray and his friends won’t be in Politics for long, and I will do everything within my power to make sure that they will not hurt the Republican Party, and our Country, again…”
The Senate will reconvene at 1:30 on Thursday.
